Berith
beh-REET
n. (Hebrew)
Hebrew b’rīth, “covenant,” possibly from a root meaning to cut (as in karat b’rīth, “to cut a covenant”) or possibly from a root meaning to bind. The Hebrew structural keyword for the binding pact between parties, especially the binding pact between God and His people.

📖 Biblical Definition

B’rīth is the great Hebrew structural noun for covenant—the binding pact, formally ratified, by which God enters into structured relationship with His people across redemptive history. The word appears about 280 times in the Old Testament, and its uses cluster into the great covenantal moments: the covenant with Noah after the flood (Gen 9:8-17), the covenant with Abraham (Gen 15, 17), the covenant at Sinai (Ex 19-24), the covenant with David (2 Sam 7), and the prophesied new covenant in Jeremiah 31:31-34 fulfilled in Christ. Each of these is a b’rīth, and each carries the structural marks of biblical covenants: a divine initiative (God comes to His people), formal stipulations (commands, promises, signs), formal ratification (often by sacrificial blood—hence karat b’rīth, “to cut a covenant,” the cutting referring to the cutting of the sacrificial victims by which the covenant was ratified), and ongoing structured relationship (the covenant community lives under the terms of its covenant). The covenant-structure is therefore the deep organizing principle of biblical theology. God does not relate to His people as the random deity of paganism, demanding propitiation now and tolerating neglect then; He relates by covenant—by formally ratified, structurally articulated, historically progressive arrangement. The history of redemption unfolds as the history of God’s covenants, each building on the one before, each pointing forward to the consummate one. The New Testament continues the structure, with diathēkē (covenant) as the Greek equivalent of b’rīth. Christ Himself at the Last Supper says: this is my blood of the new testament (diathēkē, covenant), which is shed for many for the remission of sins (Matt 26:28). Hebrews develops the doctrine at length: Christ is the mediator of a better covenant, established upon better promises, the eternal covenant whose blood is the blood of Christ. The covenant-structure is therefore not an OT-only theological curiosity but the structural reality within which the gospel itself stands: the new covenant in Christ’s blood, into which the saints are admitted by faith and baptism, under which they live with God’s law written on their hearts and the Spirit indwelling them as the seal of the covenant. The recovery of covenantal theology in any age is the recovery of the structural reality within which the gospel itself stands: a covenantal God making covenantal promises and bringing them to fulfillment in the covenantal Christ whose blood is the blood of the new covenant.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

(Hebrew term.) B’rīth: covenant; the binding pact, formally ratified, by which God enters into structured relationship with His people across redemptive history; the structural keyword of OT theology and (as Greek diathēkē) of NT theology as well.

expand to see more

COVENANT, n. — In law, a mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract. In theology, the various special arrangements by which God brings men into relation with Himself, as the covenant of works with Adam, the covenant of grace with Abraham and his seed, and the new covenant in Christ’s blood.

BERITH — (Hebrew noun, H1285.) Covenant. The structural OT keyword for the binding pact between God and His people; 285 OT occurrences. Frequently in the construct karat b’rīth, “to cut a covenant” (the cutting referring to the sacrificial victims by which the covenant was ratified).

📖 Key Scripture

Genesis 17:7 — "And I will establish my covenant between me and thee and thy seed after thee in their generations for an everlasting covenant, to be a God unto thee, and to thy seed after thee."

Jeremiah 31:31-33 — "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah... But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people."

Luke 22:20 — "Likewise also the cup after supper, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood, which is shed for you."

Hebrews 8:6 — "But now hath he obtained a more excellent ministry, by how much also he is the mediator of a better covenant, which was established upon better promises."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

B’rīth-shaped covenantal theology is corrupted, on one side, by the dispensational fragmentation that has divided redemptive history into separated dispensations with weakened covenantal continuity—and on the other by the supersessionist replacement-theology that has read the new covenant as cancelling rather than fulfilling God’s prior covenant promises, especially to Israel.

expand to see more

Strict dispensational systems have, in their classical forms, fragmented redemptive history into separated dispensations (innocence, conscience, government, promise, law, grace, kingdom) with weakened covenantal continuity between them. Each dispensation has its own administration; the church and Israel are sharply distinguished as separate peoples of God with separate covenantal trajectories; the unity of God’s covenantal dealing across redemptive history is muted. The covenantal tradition (Reformed, Presbyterian, classically Reformed Baptist) has preserved instead the structural unity: one covenant of grace, administered differently in the Old and New Testaments, fulfilled in Christ, in which the people of God (Israel under the Old, the church gathered from Jew and Gentile under the New) are essentially one. The recovery of covenantal continuity is the recovery of the structural unity of the Bible: one God making one covenant of grace, progressively unfolded across redemptive history, consummated in the one mediator Jesus Christ.

The opposite corruption is the supersessionist replacement-theology that reads the new covenant as cancelling rather than fulfilling God’s prior covenant promises, especially to Israel. The new covenant is presented as displacing the old; the Jewish people are read out of God’s purposes; the Christian church is treated as the sole heir of the promises with no remaining future role for ethnic Israel. Paul refuses this in Romans 9-11. The promises to Israel have not been annulled; the Jewish rejection of Christ has not removed Israel from God’s covenantal dealings; the future ingathering of Israel is itself part of the covenantal unfolding (and so all Israel shall be saved, Rom 11:26). Recover both ends. Refuse the dispensational fragmentation that fragments God’s covenants, and refuse the supersessionist replacement that reads the new as cancelling rather than fulfilling the prior. The biblical covenantal pattern is one God, one covenant of grace, progressively administered, consummated in Christ, with Jew and Gentile gathered into the one people of God under the new covenant Christ has ratified in His blood—and the recovery of covenantal theology in this proper form is the recovery of the structural unity within which the gospel itself stands.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew b’rīth (covenant, the binding pact); cognate verb-phrase karat b’rīth (to cut a covenant); Greek NT equivalent diathēkē—the structural keyword of biblical theology, naming the binding, formally ratified relationship by which God brings His people into structured relationship across redemptive history.

expand to see more

Hebrew b’rīth (H1285) — covenant (285 OT uses; the structural keyword of biblical theology).

Hebrew construct phrase karat b’rīth — to cut a covenant (referring to the sacrificial victims by which the covenant was ratified).

Greek diathēkē (G1242) — covenant, testament; the LXX/NT translation of b’rīth (33 NT uses).

Greek mesitēs (G3316) — mediator (of the covenant; Heb 8:6; 9:15; 12:24 of Christ as mediator of the new covenant).

"This cup is the new testament in my blood—Christ’s explicit covenantal language at the Last Supper anchors the new covenant in His own atoning death."

"Dispensational fragmentation weakens covenantal continuity; supersessionist replacement reads the new covenant as cancelling rather than fulfilling the prior; biblical covenantal theology is one God, one covenant of grace, progressively unfolded, consummated in Christ."
